about: Step 6: literal English back-translations by a model (judgment; check against the passage before quoting). The Greek's is a reference crib.
prompt: Translate the passage below into plain, literal English. Follow the passage's own wording and sentence order closely, even where that is awkward, so a reader can see what this version says rather than what Plato's Greek says. Keep the translator's choices: if the passage says "remedy", write "remedy"; if it says "means", write "means". Do not correct it toward the Greek, do not add anything, and do not smooth over omissions. If a word is damaged or uncertain (for instance by OCR), translate your best reading and mark it [?]. Return only the translation.

versions.back_translation: I heard, then, that around Naucratis of Egypt there came to be one of the old gods there, whose also the bird is sacred, which indeed they call Ibis; and his name, the daimon's itself, was Theuth. This one first found number and calculation and geometry and astronomy, and further draughts and dice, and indeed letters. And Thamus then being king of all Egypt around the great city of the upper place, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god Ammon, Theuth, having come to this one, displayed the arts, and said they must be handed out to the other Egyptians. But he asked what benefit each has, and as he went through them, as he seemed to speak well or not well, he blamed one thing and praised another. Many things indeed about each art, on both sides, Thamus is said to have declared to Theuth, which it would be a long account to go through. But when it came to letters, "This, O king, the learning," said Theuth, "will provide the Egyptians wiser and more mindful; for a remedy of memory and wisdom was found." But he said: "O most artful Theuth, one man is able to beget the things of art, but another to judge what share of harm and benefit it has for those who are going to use it. And now you, being father of letters, through good will have said the opposite of what it can do. For this will provide forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn, through neglect of memory, inasmuch as through trust in writing they are reminded from outside by alien marks, not from inside themselves by themselves. So not of memory but of reminding you found a remedy. And of wisdom you provide to the students opinion, not truth. For having become hearers of many things by you without teaching, they will seem to be knowers of many things, being, for the most part, without knowledge, and hard to be with, having become seeming-wise instead of wise."

I heard that near Egyptian Naucratis lived one of the ancient gods of that place, to whom was consecrated the bird called the ibis. The name of this deity — Theut[172]. He first invented number, arithmetic, geometry and astronomy, the game of draughts and dice, and invented [107]also letters. King of all Egypt at that time was D. Famus[173], who sat in a large city of the upper part of the country. This city the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god — Ammon. Once Theut, having come to Famus, announced to him his arts and said that it was necessary to communicate them to all the Egyptians; but the latter asked him: what use can each of them provide? When Theut began to explain this, the king, depending on whether the explanation appeared to him good or bad, censured some things and praised others. In general, he said much to Theut E. about each art, in the one direction and the other: to tell about this would take long. Finally the matter came to letters, and Theut said: Sovereign! this science will make the Egyptians wiser and more mindful; I invented it as a means for memory and wisdom. But the king answered: Much-learned Theut! one is able to give birth to arts, and another to judge how much harm or profit they will bring to the people who will use them. Here you, father of letters, from 275. parental love, have ascribed to them the opposite of what they can do. For this, weakening carefulness about remembering, will produce in the souls of the pupils forgetfulness[174]; because, relying on external writing, depicted by foreign signs, they will not recall impressions internally — themselves in [108]themselves. So you have invented a means not for remembering, but for reminding. And wisdom the pupils will acquire[175] from you not true, but seeming; because, having listened to much and studying nothing, they will represent themselves as knowers of much and, as supposed sages, instead of true ones, B. will remain for the most part ignorant and people in society unbearable.

I heard, then, that near Naukratis in Egypt there lived one of the old gods of that place, to whom the bird too is dedicated, called the Ibis. And the god himself was said to be called Teut. He was said to have been the first to invent numbers and reckonings, geometry and astronomy, further draughts and the game of dice, and besides that, letters. King of the whole of Egypt was at that time Tamuz, and he reigned in that great city in Upper Egypt which the Greeks call the Egyptian Thebes, and the god they call Ammon. To him, then, came Teut, taught him his arts and told him to spread them among the other Egyptians. And he asked what benefit each of them would bring, and then, as Teut's words seemed to him right or not right, one thing he blamed and another he praised. About each art Tamuz had much good and much bad to say to Teut, about which it would take long to tell. Well, when they came to letters, Teut said to Tamuz: "King, this learning will make the Egyptians wiser and more capable in remembering; this invention is a remedy for memory and wisdom." And he said to him in answer: "Teut, most accomplished master! One person is able to beget what belongs to an art, and another is able to judge for what it may be useful and in what harmful to those who will want to make use of a given art. So also now: you are the father of letters, therefore out of good heart for them you have ascribed to them a value directly opposite to the one which they truly possess. This invention will sow forgetfulness in human souls, because a man who learns this will cease to exercise memory; he will trust writing and will recall everything from outside, from signs foreign to his being, and not from his own interior, from himself. So this is not a remedy for memory, but only a means for recalling to oneself. To your pupils you will give only the appearance of wisdom, and not true wisdom. For they will possess great well-readness without learning and it will seem to them that they know much, and for the most part they will know nothing and only to associate with them will be hard; these will be wise men in appearance, and not people wise in truth."

Olen siis kuullut,[74] että Naukratiin lähellä Egyptissä eli muuan sikäläisistä vanhoista jumalista, jolle on pyhitetty lintukin, jota he kutsuvat Ibikseksi.

I have heard, then,[74] that near Naucratis in Egypt lived one of the old gods of that place, to whom a bird too has been consecrated, which they call the Ibis. The god's own name was Theuth. He first invented number and the art of calculation, geometry and astronomy, further board-games and dice-games, and so also letters. The king of all Egypt then was Thamus, in the upper land, in a great city which the Hellenes call the Egyptian Thebes, just as they call the god Ammon. To him came Theuth, displayed his skills, and said that they should be distributed to the other Egyptians. He asked then what benefit each had, and as the other was presenting, he now blamed, now praised, according as Theuth seemed to speak rightly or wrongly. And of Thamus it is said that on each skill he uttered extensive judgments in both directions, which it would become too long to present precisely. But when he was at the letters, Theuth said: "This learning, O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and better in their memory, for it has been invented as an auxiliary means for memory and for wisdom." The latter answered: "Most skilful Theuth! Some are able to give birth to what belongs to the skills, others again to judge what large share of benefit, and what large share of harm, results from it for those who have to use it. So you, the father of letters, out of attachment to them have presented quite the opposite of what they bring about. For in the souls of those who learn this skill, it produces forgetfulness, for the reason that they neglect memory, because, trusting in writing, they bring things back to their mind from outside, by the influence of foreign marks, not from inside, from themselves. So you have not invented an auxiliary instrument for memory, but for recalling to mind. And only a broken-wisdom do you provide for the pupils, not true wisdom. For having heard much without instruction, they believe themselves to be many-knowing, although for the most part they are ignorant and tiresome in company, having become broken-wise instead of having become wise."

I heard, then, that around Naucratis (72) in Egypt there was born one of the old gods there, whose sacred bird is the one they call ibis. The name of this god is Theuth. He first found both number and calculation and geometry and astronomy, and besides the games with draughtsmen and dice, and finally writing as well. At that time Thamus was king of all Egypt, living in the great city of the upper place, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and its god Ammon (73). Theuth went to him, set out his arts, and maintained that they ought to be spread to the other Egyptians. Thamus asked him which benefit each art provides. While Theuth was developing his inventions, the other blamed some and praised others. But a long speech would be needed for us to go through the many arguments, for or against each art, that Thamus is said to have declared to Theuth. When he reached writing, Theuth said: "This lesson, O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and more mindful of memory, because the remedy of memory and of wisdom has been found." Thamus answered: "Most inventive Theuth, one man has the power to devise the art, and another to judge what part of benefit harm those who are going to apply the art will receive. And now you, because you are the father of letters and are disposed favorably toward your work, have said a judgment opposite to its real power. For this will provide forgetfulness in the souls of those who learn, because the exercise of the mnemonic will be neglected, since, having confidence in writing, they remember things from the outside through foreign elements and not from their interior themselves by themselves. So you did not find a remedy of memory, but of reminding. And to the students you provide imaginary wisdom and not truth. For having read many things without teaching, they will imagine that they are very learned, while for the most part they are unlearned and unbearable in their relations, because they will have become, instead of wise, seeming-wise."

I have heard it said that near Naucratis[55], in Egypt, there was a god, one of the most anciently worshipped in the country, and the very one to whom the bird that is called Ibis is consecrated. This god is called Theuth[56]. They say that he first invented numbers, calculation, [274d] geometry and astronomy; the games of chess, of dice, and writing. All of Egypt was then under the rule of Thamus, who lived in the great capital city of upper Egypt; the Greeks call the city Thebes the Egyptian, and the god, Ammon[57]. Theuth therefore came to find the king, showed him the arts he had invented, and told him that they must be shared with all the Egyptians. The latter asked him of what use each of these arts would be, and set about discoursing on everything Theuth said on the subject of his inventions, [274e] blaming this, approving that. Thus Thamus put forward, they say, to the god Theuth many reasons for and against each art in particular. It would be too long to go through them; but when they came to writing: "This science, O king!" Theuth said to him, "will render the Egyptians more learned and will relieve their memory. It is a remedy that I have found against the difficulty of learning and of knowing." The king replied: "Industrious Theuth, one man is capable of giving birth to the arts, another of appraising the advantages or the disadvantages that may result from their use; [275a] and you, father of writing, through a natural kindness toward your work, have seen it quite other than it is: it will produce only forgetfulness in the mind of those who learn, by making them neglect memory. In effect, they will leave to these foreign characters the care of reminding them of what they have entrusted to writing, and will themselves keep no remembrance of it. You have therefore not found a means for memory, but for simple reminiscence, and you offer your disciples only the name of science without the reality; for, when they have read many things [275b] without masters, they will believe themselves to have numerous knowledges, ignorant as they will be for the most part, and the false opinion they will have of their science will render them insupportable in the commerce of life."

I have therefore heard it said that there existed near Naucratis, in Egypt, one of the ancient gods of that country, and that to this god the Egyptians consecrated the bird which they called ibis. This god was named Theuth. It is he who first invented the science of numbers, calculation, geometry, astronomy, backgammon, dice, and finally writing. King Thamous was then reigning over the whole country; he lived in the great city of Upper Egypt which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, as they name Ammon the god-king Thamous. Theuth therefore came to find this king in order to show him the arts which he had invented, and he told him that they must be spread among the Egyptians. The king asked him of what utility each of the arts would be. The god informed him; and, according as he judged them to be a good or an evil, the king approved or blamed. It is said that Thamous made to Theuth many observations for and against each art. It would be too long to set them out. But, when they came to writing: "King, said Theuth to him, this science will render the Egyptians more learned and will facilitate the art of remembering, for I have found a remedy to relieve science and memory." And the king replied: "Most ingenious Theuth, one man is capable of creating the arts, and another is in a position to judge what lot of utility or of harmfulness they will confer on those who make use of them. And it is thus that you, father of writing, attribute to it, out of benevolence, quite the contrary of what it can bring. [275] It can produce in souls, in effect, only the forgetting of what they know by making them neglect memory. Because they will have faith in writing, it is from outside, by foreign imprints, and no longer from within and from the depth of themselves, that men will seek to remember. You have found the means, not at all of enriching memory, but of preserving the memories which it has. You give to your disciples the presumption that they have science, not science itself. When they will have, in effect, learned much without a master, they will imagine themselves become very learned, and they will be for the most part only ignorant people of troublesome company, imaginary learned men instead of true learned men."

I have heard, then, that at Naucratis in Egypt there was one of the old gods there, to whom also the bird that is called Ibis was sacred, but he himself, the god, was called Theuth. This one is said to have first invented number and reckoning, then the art of measuring and the science of the stars, further the board game and the dice game, and so also the letters. As king of all Egypt there had ruled at that time Thamus, in the great city of the upper land, which the Hellenes call the Egyptian Thebes, but the god himself Ammon. To him Theuth went, showed him his arts, and requested that they might be communicated to the other Egyptians. That one asked what use each one provided, and according as what Theuth put forward about it seemed to him right or not right, he blamed or praised. Much now Thamus is said to have said to Theuth about each art, for it and against it, which it would be lengthy to cite all. But when he had come to the letters, Theuth said: This art, O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and richer in memory, for as a means for the understanding and the memory it has been invented. But that one replied: O most art-rich Theuth, one person knows how to bring to light what belongs to the arts; another, to judge how much harm and advantage they bring to those who will use them (275). So you too now, as father of the letters, out of love have said the opposite of what they bring about. For this invention will instill in the souls of those who learn rather forgetfulness, out of neglect of memory, because, in trust in writing, they will remember only from outside by means of foreign signs, but not inwardly themselves and immediately. Not, then, for memory, but only for reminding have you invented a means, and of wisdom you impart to your pupils only the appearance, not the thing itself. For since they will have heard much without instruction, they will also seem to themselves to be knowing-of-much, though they are for the most part ignorant, and hard to deal with, after they have become conceited-wise instead of wise.

Ich habe also vernommen — I have heard, then, that in Naukratis in Egypt there was one of the old gods there, to whom also the holy bird, which they indeed call Ibis, belonged; the demon himself, however, had the name Theuth. This one, it is said, first invented number and reckoning, and mathematics and star-knowledge, further board game and dice game, indeed even also the letters. Further, however, since at that time over all Egypt Thamus was king in the great city of the upper district, which the Hellenes call the Egyptian Thebes, as they call the god there Ammon, – so Theuth came to this one and showed him his arts and said that one must now communicate them to the other Egyptians. But he asked what kind of use each one had? As he now explained it, he knew, as it seemed to him that that one said something good or not good, to blame it now, to praise it now. Much, now, Thamus is said there to have said to Theuth about each art, in both directions, frankly, which to go through would require many words. But when he was at the letters, Theuth said: "This knowledge, O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and more capable of remembering; for as an aid for remembering as well as for wisdom it is invented." But he replied: "O you very artful[474] Theuth! Another is the one who, to bring forth what belongs to the art, another however the one who is able to judge what share of harm as well as of use it may bring to those who will use it. So have also you now, as father of the letters, out of fatherly love said the opposite of what their effect is. For forgetfulness this will bring about in the souls of those who get to know it, through neglect of remembering, inasmuch as they now, in trust in the writing, from outside by means of foreign signs, not from inside out of themselves, draw remembering. Not, then, for remembering, but for the memory have you invented an aid. Of wisdom, however, you offer the pupils only appearance, not truth. For many-hearers are they to you now without instruction, and so they will think themselves to be many-knowers, since they are yet commonly know-nothings and people with whom it is hard to get along, in that they have become seeming-wise, not wise."

I have heard it told, then, that in the vicinity of Naucrate of Egypt there was one of the ancient Gods of that place, the one to whom the bird they call Ibis is sacred, and that this divinity had the name of Tot[41], and that he had first found numbers and calculation and geometry and astronomy, and besides this chess, dice and writing. Tamo being in those days king of all Egypt, in that great city of upper Egypt which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and they call the God Ammon, Tot having come to the [p. 101 edit] presence of this man, showed him the arts, and said to him that it was necessary to make a gift of them to the rest of the Egyptians. And the king asked what utility each of them had: and he showing it, the king, according as it seemed to him that he spoke well or badly, disapproved or approved: and they say that Tamo brought to Tot many reasons for and against for each art, which to relate them would be too long. But when it came to the letters: O king, said Tot, this teaching will render the Egyptians wiser and more mindful, because I have found this aid for knowledge and for memory. And the king said: O most ingenious Tot, one man will be able to create the arts, another man to judge what part of harm or of utility they have for him who makes use of them; and you now, being as the father of the written letters, through the love you bear to them, have said that which they cannot do, whereas writing will bring forgetfulness into the mind of him who learns it and will cause the exercise of memory to be neglected, because men, trusting themselves to the written letters, do not remember by a working that they do within themselves, but by the external aid of foreign signs, so that you have not found a means of retaining, but of recalling to memory things; hence to your disciples you give an apparent wisdom and not the true, because having heard many things, they become without a teacher, in appearance, learned in [p. 102 edit] many things, whereas they are for the most part ignorant; and they will be tiresome to those who deal with them, since instead of being wise, they will have only the appearance.

I need to correct that: I must return only the translation, in English. Here it is:

They told me that near Naucratis{31}, in Egypt, there was a God, one of the most ancient of the country, the same one to which the bird that the Egyptians call Ibis is consecrated. This God was called Teut{32}. It is said that he invented numbers, calculation, geometry, astronomy, as well as the games of chess and of dice, and, in short, writing. The king Tamus reigned then over all that country, and lived in the great city of upper Egypt, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and which is, under the protection of the God whom they call Ammon. Teut presented himself to the king and showed him the arts that he had invented, and told him how convenient it was to extend them among the Egyptians. The king asked him of what utility each one of them would be, and Teut went explaining to him in detail the uses of each one; and according as the explanations seemed to him more or less satisfactory, Tamus approved or disapproved. It is said that the king alleged to the inventor, in each one of the inventions, many reasons for and against, which it would be long to enumerate. When they arrived at writing: "O king!, Teut said to him, this invention will make the [341] Egyptians wiser and will serve their memory; I have discovered a remedy against the difficulty of learning and retaining{33}." "Ingenious Teut, the king responded, the genius that invents the arts is not in the case that the wisdom that appreciates the advantages and the disadvantages that must result from their application. Father of writing and enthused with your invention, you attribute to it the whole contrary of its true effects. It will produce nothing but forgetfulness in the souls of those who know it, making them despise memory; trusting in this foreign aid they will abandon to material characters the care of preserving the memories, whose trace their spirit will have lost. You have not found a means of cultivating memory, but of awakening reminiscences; and you give your disciples the shadow of science and not science itself. Because, when they see that they can learn many things without teachers, they will already take themselves for wise, and they will be nothing more than ignorant, for the most part, and unbearable false wise men in the commerce of life."

I have heard indeed, around Naucratis of Egypt, that there was a certain one of the ancient Gods, to whom a bird is dedicated, which they call Ibis; but to the daemon himself the name Theuth. That this one first invented number and the computation of numbers, and geometry, and astronomy; again the game of knucklebones and of dice, and letters. There was then king of all Egypt Thamus, and in the most eminent and most ample city, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes; and the God himself they call Ammon. To this one Theuth, having set out, showed his arts, and said that they ought to be distributed next to the other Egyptians. But he asked what the utility of each would be; and, he himself reporting, what seemed well said, he approved indeed; what on the contrary, he censured. Where Thamus is reported to have shown to Theuth many things about any art whatever in each direction, of which, if we proceed to narrate the individual ones, the speech will be more prolix. But when they had come down to letters, "This discipline," said Theuth, "O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and more memorious. For this has been invented as a remedy of memory and of wisdom." But he said: "O most artful Theuth, one indeed is suitable for fabricating the works of an art, another more ready for judging what of advantage or of harm they are going to bring to those using. And yet you also, father of letters, on account of benevolence, have affirmed the contrary of what they are able to effect. For the use of them, on account of negligence of recollection, will produce forgetfulness in the mind of those learning; inasmuch as they, trusting in the external monuments of letters, will not revolve the things themselves within in the mind. Wherefore not of memory, but of commemoration, a remedy you have found. Of wisdom also the opinion rather than the truth you hand over to the disciples. For when they will have read through many things without the teaching of a teacher, experts of many [multaram: many? [?]] things in the common view, although they are ignorant, they will seem. In association also they will be more troublesome, as those who are not endowed with wisdom itself, but furnished with the opinion of wisdom."
